nameStory: This lichen gets its "map" name from the way it creates intricate patterns on rock surfaces that look remarkably like the boundaries on a topographic map. The patches of lichen are separated by dark lines, just like countries or states on an atlas. The "subgeminatum" part of its scientific name means "almost twinned," referring to how its reproductive structures often appear nearly paired together.
description: This is a crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches directly on rock surfaces, looking like someone splashed yellow-green paint that dried and cracked. The lichen grows as irregular patches that can spread several inches across, with a distinctive network of dark lines creating a map-like pattern. It's one of the map lichens, a group known for their slow growth and incredibly long lifespans. **Note: Identification details are uncertain due to limited reference material - this species is rarely documented in New England.**

idTips.label: Map-like Pattern
idTips.description: Look for yellow-green patches broken up by dark, irregular lines that create a geographic map appearance on rock surfaces

idTips.label: Rock-hugging Growth
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that feels rough like fine sandpaper and is impossible to peel off the rock without tools

idTips.label: Color Variations
idTips.description: Ranges from bright yellow-green when wet to pale greenish-gray when dry, with the dark boundary lines always remaining visible

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Small, dark, button-like dots (apothecia) may appear on the surface, often in nearly paired arrangements

habitat: **Habitat details are uncertain** - likely found on exposed granite, quartzite, or other hard rock surfaces in mountainous areas of New England. Based on related species, probably prefers acidic rocks in areas with clean air, potentially at higher elevations in the White Mountains or similar rocky outcrops.

seasonality.spring: **Seasonal details uncertain** - likely most visible when spring rains make the lichen more vibrant and easier to spot against dark, wet rock surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Probably appears more muted and grayish during dry periods, but the distinctive map pattern should remain clearly visible on rock faces.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture may revive the yellow-green coloration, making this a good time for identification before winter weather.
seasonality.winter: May be obscured by snow and ice, but could be visible on south-facing rock surfaces that remain exposed during mild periods.

funFact: **This fact is uncertain due to limited data** - Map lichens are among the slowest-growing organisms on Earth, with some colonies potentially living for thousands of years and growing less than a millimeter per year, making them living archives of environmental history.
confusionNotes: **Comparison details uncertain** - Most easily confused with the much more common Yellow Map Lichen, but the specific distinguishing features of this rare species are not well documented. The nearly paired reproductive structures suggested by its name may be a key difference.
contextualKnowledge: **This information is uncertain** - This species appears to be extremely rare in New England with only one documented observation, so any sighting would be scientifically significant and worth reporting to local naturalist groups or iNaturalist for expert verification.
compareHints: **Comparison details uncertain due to rarity** - Differs from Yellow Map Lichen in having reproductive structures that appear nearly paired (suggested by "subgeminatum"), and likely differs from Twin Map Lichen in subtle microscopic features. However, distinguishing this rare species from its relatives may require expert examination and possibly microscopic analysis.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Yellow map lichen stands out from its map lichen relatives by its bright yellow-green color and classic map-like appearance with clear black borders.
Unlike the famous Yellow Map Lichen which maintains distinct, separate patches with clear boundaries, Crescent Map Lichen merges into continuous carpets across rock surfaces.
Twin Map Lichen is distinguished from Yellow Map Lichen primarily by its paired spores versus single spores, though they look nearly identical otherwise.
Unlike the more common Yellow Map Lichen which tends to be bright yellow-green, Single-spored Map Lichen often shows more varied coloration.
